summary: The article provides a generally accurate overview of NRI home loans, RBI rate hikes, and the considerations for down payments versus overseas savings, with most claims aligning with authoritative sources.

claims.claim: When the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) increases its key policy rates, like the repo rate, it essentially makes it more expensive for banks to borrow money. This cost is then passed on to consumers in the form of higher interest rates on various loans, including home loans.
claims.note: RBI repo rate changes directly impact home loan interest rates and EMIs. When the RBI increases the repo rate, banks pass on the higher borrowing cost to customers, leading to higher EMIs for floating-rate home loans.

claims.claim: When inflation is high, the RBI typically raises the repo rate – the rate at which commercial banks borrow money from the central bank. The primary reason for an RBI rate hike is to curb inflation. By making borrowing more expensive, the RBI aims to reduce the money supply in the economy, thereby cooling demand and bringing down price increases.
claims.note: Controlling inflation is one of the main objectives of monetary policy. When the central bank wishes to combat inflation, it will increase the repo rate as it will discourage commercial banks from arranging funds from the central bank, and thus lesser funds are available with the central bank to disburse as loans.

claims.claim: Most home loans in India, especially floating rate ones, are linked to external benchmarks like the RBI's repo rate (Repo Linked Lending Rate or RLLR).
claims.note: Floating-rate home loans are directly linked to the repo rate.

claims.claim: While repatriating funds from NRE (Non-Resident External) accounts to India for a home loan down payment is generally tax-free, any interest earned on NRE accounts is also tax-exempt in India.
claims.note: Interest earned on an NRE account is tax-free in India under Section 10(4)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, as long as the residential status remains Non-Resident.

claims.claim: It's essential to understand the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) between India and your country of residence to avoid paying taxes twice.
claims.note: The Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) is a treaty signed between two or more countries to prevent individuals and businesses from being taxed twice on the same income.

article_title: NRI Home Loans: Down Payment vs. Overseas Savings Post-RBI Hike
